title: U.S. measles cases surpass last year's total: Tracker
description: The U.S. measles case count for this year has surged past last year's total and now stands at 2,295 — a level that hasn't been seen in 35 years, according to a Johns Hopkins University tracker that compiles state and local health data. Why it matters: It's the latest sign that the virus is rebounding in areas with low vaccine coverage, threatening the United States' measles elimination status , which is due to be reviewed in November. The big picture : The majority of cases are in unvaccinated people. While overall measles vaccination rates are still relatively high, public health officials say they must remain above 95% to maintain herd immunity. By the numbers: As of Tuesday, there were nine more cases than all of 2025 , per the Johns Hopkins U.S. measles tracker. Jurisdictions including South Carolina, Utah, Texas, Florida and Arizona have the most reported cases. The Centers for Disease Control reported 2,260 confirmed cases in its last update on July 16. The agency said there were 34 new outbreaks reported this year. The last time measles cases were higher was in 1991, when the U.S. had 9,643 cases, according to CDC data . Threat level: Measles symptoms include a cough, high fever and conjunctivitis as well as a telltale rash, but can escalate into complications such as severe ear infections, pneumonia and encephalitis or inflammation of the brain that can lead to permanent brain damage and even death, per Johns Hopkins Medicine. On average, measles kills between one and three of every 1,000 infected children. The rebound comes at a time when a number of key top government health positions — including CDC director and surgeon general — remain vacant and after Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. initially downplayed the virus' threat. He's since said the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles spread while noting vaccination is a personal choice.

title: Senate rabble-rousers are gaining power
description: Hardline conservatives are gaining power in the Senate atop key committees. Why it matters: The senators known for rankling GOP leadership now have gavels that let them hold hearings, advance legislation and even issue subpoenas. Driving the news: Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) will be the new chair of the Budget Committee, Senate Republicans agreed in their closed-door lunch Tuesday. The committee, which has a key role in reconciliation, had been chaired by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) Johnson also chairs the Homeland Security subcommittee on investigations, allowing him to launch probes into everything from former President Biden's health to Meta's alleged cooperation with China. What to watch: Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) is next in line to take the gavel on the powerful Judiciary Committee next Congress, following Graham's death and Sen. John Cornyn's (R-Texas) primary loss. Lee would have to forfeit his current Energy Committee chair post. He indicated to the Washington Examiner he would be willing to do so. Zoom out: Fiscal hawk Rand Paul (R-Ky.) chairs the Homeland Security Committee, where he has been skeptical of massive agency budgets. He recently voted "no" on Markwayne Mullin's nomination to be DHS secretary. Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) chairs the Aging Committee, and he also leads the GOP steering committee, an unofficial, conservative group. Scott has leveraged the group's weekly lunch to bring in top government officials, including President Trump, to discuss current issues. The bottom line: The Senate runs on seniority. That means even senators willing to buck their party or criticize leadership can climb committee ranks.

title: Scoop: Progressives scorch Gillibrand over crypto
description: Progressive groups are opening a vicious new front in the fight over crypto legislation , targeting Sen Kirsten Gillibrand as she tries to broker a compromise on the CLARITY Act, which has unresolved issues on its ethics provisions. Why it matters: The blistering — and deeply personal — attack from Indivisible, Demand Progress and the Revolving Door Project complicates already delicate negotiations. It's also a warning shot to Democrats: Progressive groups are prepared to make support for the bill politically painful, even if it means another bruising intraparty fight over one of the crypto industry's top legislative priorities. "Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), is a prime example of a Democratic leader whose conduct undermines efforts to hold the Trump administration accountable for their rampant corruption," the groups wrote in a letter sent to every Democratic Senate office Tuesday evening. "Fair or not, criticisms of the Trump administration's overwhelming corruption fall flat when voters perceive the critics to be engaged in substantively similar behavior." The groups argue that Gillibrand's son's involvement in the crypto industry leaves Democrats vulnerable to the very charge they are trying to level against President Trump. Trump's crypto ventures have generated an estimated $600 million windfall, testing long-standing norms around presidents profiting from businesses affected by government decisions. The other side: Gillibrand has called for Congress to prevent all elected officials, and their spouses, from issuing or sponsoring their own digital assets. "This is a commonsense requirement that should get broad bipartisan support — public officials and their spouses should not be issuing memecoins," she said in a June statement. State of play: Finding 60 votes for the CLARITY Act this summer is a high-wire act, but passing the bill remains a top priority for Senate Republicans, the White House and the crypto industry. Sens. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) are working with the White House on compromise language for the ethics provisions. They appear to be making progress, though the details of the compromise haven't been released. In addition to the talks with the White House, bipartisan talks are underway, with Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) leading Republicans in negotiating the ethics language. The intrigue: Looming over the negotiations is the crypto industry's political war chest. Fairshake, its flagship super PAC, has some $125 million on hand. The industry's political muscle gives both parties another incentive to reach a deal — and another reason for progressives to dig in. Republicans are eager to put that money to work to help defend their Senate majority, but — as with the legislative negotiations — the clock is ticking for those dollars to have maximum impact in the midterm elections. What we're hearing: Both parties view the ethics language as the biggest remaining obstacle to securing the 60 votes needed to pass the CLARITY Act. The bill cleared the Senate Banking Committee in May with support from two Democrats, Sens. Ruben Gallego (Ariz.) and Angela Alsobrooks (Md.), underscoring the bill's bipartisan potential and the difficult coalition it will take to reach the Senate floor. Zoom out: Crypto regulation continues to divide Democrats on both policy and politics. Last year's passage of the GENIUS Act — which established the first federal regulatory framework for dollar-backed stablecoins — sparked tense internal Democratic debates over both the merits of the legislation and Trump's financial ties to the crypto industry. In the end, 18 Senate Democrats voted for the bill.

description: Sunday's FIFA World Cup final drew more than 62.8 million viewers in the U.S., making it the most-watched World Cup final and soccer telecast in American history. Why it matters: The record audience underscores soccer's growing popularity in the U.S. and is likely to boost the value of future media rights. By the numbers: The game , which saw Spain beat defending champion Argentina 1–0 in extra time, also was the most-watched soccer match in Spanish-language media history, Telemundo said. Nearly 39 million U.S. viewers watched the game on Fox, which had exclusive English-language broadcast rights in the U.S. Those figures are up 132% from the 2022 final on Fox, the company said . Another nearly 24 million U.S. viewers tuned into the broadcast on Telemundo, which had exclusive Spanish-language broadcast rights in the U.S. Those figures are up 166% from the 2022 final on Telemundo. Data: Nielsen; Note: Includes English and Spanish broadcasts. Nielsen began including out-of-home and streaming viewing in its official national TV ratings in 2020; Chart: Kerry Flynn/Axios Streaming played a big role in the tournament's reach. June was the biggest subscriber acquisition month for Fox's streaming service, Fox One, according to Antenna . Fox One added an estimated 2.8 million new subscribers in June, more than 2.5 times its previous monthly record in January during the NFL playoffs, per Antenna. Nearly all of Fox's new June subscribers — 93% — were first-time customers rather than returning users. The intrigue: Peacock, which streams Telemundo, also saw strong subscriber growth, recording an estimated 3.75 million U.S. sign-ups in June, per Antenna. Streaming accounted for nearly half of Telemundo's World Cup audience, up from 30% in 2022, per Telemundo. Telemundo's coverage resonated beyond Spanish speakers, as some preferred the energetic commentary , lack of commercials during the hydration breaks and cheaper cost of Peacock compared to Fox One. Between the lines: America hosting the tournament, a competitive U.S. men's national team and broader streaming distribution helped push viewership to new heights in the U.S. The U.S. team's matches set audience records. Fox said the U.S. opening match against Paraguay on June 12 became the most-watched FIFA Men's World Cup telecast in English-language U.S. history, averaging 18 million viewers. The U.S. men's victory over Bosnia and Herzegovina on July 1 set the record as the biggest English-language TV audience for any soccer match in America with 26.4 million viewers on Fox. The U.S. team's loss to Belgium on July 6 later bested the record with 37.2 million viewers on Fox, per Nielsen, along with 12.9 million viewers on Telemundo, for more than 50 million combined. The July 5 match between Mexico and England came close to that record with 46.7 million viewers on Fox and Telemundo. The big picture: The FIFA World Cup has historically attracted the largest global audience of any recurring television event worldwide. FIFA has not yet released worldwide figures. The 2022 World Cup final between Argentina and France held the previous final game viewership record at 1.42 billion worldwide, per FIFA . Live sports remain one of the few programming categories capable of attracting massive live audiences , driving both advertising revenue and streaming subscriptions. FIFA also experimented with bringing more American-style entertainment to the event, including its first halftime show for a World Cup final, to help the tournament appeal beyond traditional soccer fans. What to watch: FIFA is expected to cash in on the tournament's success by opening up the media rights bidding process for the 2030 World Cup. Fox and Telemundo's current agreements ran through the 2026 tournament, after FIFA extended the deals without a competitive bidding process for the 2022 tournament. FIFA has reportedly alerted media companies that English- and Spanish-language U.S. rights are likely to be sold together as a package for 2030, per CNBC , with Netflix, Disney and YouTube all interested in bidding.
